metadata.title: PISA 2022 Results Volume III: Creative Minds, Creative Schools Factsheets Indonesia

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This factsheet reports PISA 2022 results for Indonesia using the OECD PISA 2022 Database. The underlying PISA design is a complex, multi-stage sampling of schools and students, and OECD reporting typically relies on sampling weights to produce population-representative estimates for 15-year-olds. The factsheet does not specify the exact weight variable name(s) (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used, so the precise weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Plausible values are used for PISA cognitive achievement scales in the OECD database, but this factsheet presents summary statistics and correlations rather than detailing the PV-combining procedure.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The provided factsheet text does not describe how plausible values (PVs) for the PISA creative thinking scale were combined (e.g., Rubin’s rules vs. PV averaging), nor does it document a missing-data strategy for the analytic estimates. This is a reporting gap for methodological transparency: the factsheet focuses on descriptive and comparative results rather than the technical estimation details. Given that PISA cognitive outcomes are typically PV-based, PV handling and missing-data procedures are expected to be specified in the OECD technical documentation, but they are not included in the excerpt.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Indonesia PISA 2022 creative thinking factsheet sample: 13,439 students in 410 schools who completed the assessment in mathematics, reading or science, and for whom creative thinking results are reported for the 15-year-old population in Indonesia. The excerpt does not specify additional exclusions (e.g., missing background questionnaire items) or any further task-level completion filters beyond the stated assessment participation.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 Volume III factsheet summarizes Indonesia’s performance on the PISA Creative Thinking cognitive test for 15-year-olds. The creative thinking assessment contains 32 open-ended tasks measuring three ideation processes (generating diverse ideas, generating creative ideas, evaluating and improving ideas) across four domain contexts (written expression, visual expression, social problem solving, scientific problem solving). For Indonesia, the mean creative thinking score is 19 on a 60-point scale, which is significantly below the OECD average (33). Only 31% of students reach at least Level 3 (baseline proficiency), while 5% are top performers at Levels 5–6. The factsheet also reports within-Indonesia performance gaps by socio-economic status and gender, and it describes how creative thinking relates to mathematics and reading performance (correlations of 0.57 and 0.55, respectively). Methodological details on PV combining and missing-data handling are not provided in the excerpt, limiting reproducibility of the exact estimation procedure.
